newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada to see moderate growth in 1997 - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Canada to see moderate growth in 1997 - OECD.

text.p: The pace of Canada's economy growth will pick up in 1997, boosted by positive economic and fiscal fundamentals, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said in a report released Monday.

In its semi-annual outlook on Canada, the OECD said continuing fiscal restraint and a slower than expected expansion in the United States would not be enough to slow down growth. The organisation forecast the pace of economic expansion in Canada to more than double next year.
The OECD saw gross domestic product (GDP) at market prices rising 1.5 percent this year and forecast it more than doubling to 3.3 percent in 1997. In 1995 GDP grew 2.3 percent.
But it pegged Canada's unemployment rate at 9.6 percent in 1996 and at 9.4 percent in 1997, still well above the OECD average.

The OECD noted Canada's low inflation and continuing fiscal consolidation at both federal and provincial levels which had created the conditions for the lowest interest rates in the country in decades.

The organisation said interest rate-sensitive industries have benefitted from this and have stepped up job creation. But declines in public sector employment together with a growing labour force have offset such gains, keeping the unemployment rate at a relatively high 9.5 percent to 10 percent level.

Inflation in Canada was likely to remain in the lower half of the central bank's 1 percent to 3 percent target range, the OECD said, largely due to the slack in the labour market, as well as Canada's widening output gap.

The country's favourable inflation performance, together with its increased competitiveness in export markets and slower import growth have brought about a marked improvement in Canada's current account, the widest measure of trade.
Canada posted current account trade surpluses in the second and third quarters this year, marking the first such development since 1984.

The OECD also said that Canada's low inflation, progress in cutting federal and provincial deficits and the reduced threat of Quebec separatism have increased financial markets' confidence in the country and have contributed to a more stable Canadian dollar.
"This has allowed the Bank of Canada to lower short-term interest rates to levels well below those prevailing in the United States," the OECD said.

The OECD said its projections were based on the assumption that the economic fundamentals would allow the Bank of Canada not to follow an eventual modest increase in interest rates in the United States.
This should lead to further declines in long-term interest rates, eventually bringing Canadian rates below their U.S. counterparts.
The organisation said Canada's public debt-to-GDP ratio should begin to decline in 1997 but that it would be a while before it approaches the OECD average.

"With fiscal restraint ongoing and the cyclical component of the deficit declining, general government finances (on a national acocunts basis) are projected by the OECD Secretariat to approach balance by the end of 1998," the organisation said.
